summary: Dedicated pool throughput collapse during mixed small-stream + large-batch surge (intermittent autoscale throttling)
description:
Issue summary: Nimbus Travel reports repeated p99 latency spikes and end-to-end throughput collapse in their dedicated pool when a surge of short, latency-sensitive streaming requests overlaps with scheduled large-batch offline jobs. Impact: multiple customer endpoints experienced sustained 5–10x p99 latency increases over a 45-minute window; user-facing timeouts and retry storms. Environment: Dedicated GPU pool (nid-dedicated-37) in prod-us-west running mixed tenant workloads pinned to reserved capacity. Observed at 2026-03-10 02:15–03:00 UTC.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Simulate steady-state small-stream traffic (~200 rps, avg payload short). 2) Launch a scheduled batch job that performs long sequence generation (many tokens, large batch sizes) on the same pool for ~30–60 minutes. 3) Observe autoscaler behavior and queueing/backpressure; monitor p99 latency and GPU utilization.

Logs/metrics: customer-side traces show streaming sessions stall at connection flush during batch ramp; backend metrics show sudden increase in kernel queue depth, reduction in concurrent slot availability, autoscaler issued scale-up requests but several were denied/throttled with "capacity-queue-timeout" in allocator logs. GPU memory fragmentation increased during the period; scheduler logs show repeated preemption/reshuffle attempts.

Impact notes: This is customer-visible and reproducible in our internal repro cluster using a mixed small + large workload profile. The problem differs from simple noisy-tenant CPU hogging: the failure mode appears tied to allocator slot serialization and autoscaler admission controls that prevent timely transient scale-ups when the pool has many small streaming sessions interleaving with high-memory batch allocations.
investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: the autoscaler admission policy had a hard lower bound on slot consolidation which caused it to defer scaling until batch jobs freed contiguous GPU banks; meanwhile small streams hold many thin slots that block allocation of large contiguous blocks for long-batch kernels. Evidence: allocator trace at 2026-03-10T02:22 shows requests queued behind small-stream KV cache locks; scale-up requests were rate-limited by the control-plane policy ('scope:reserved:burst_limit'). Repro: we ran a synthetic test in staging -> reproduced p99 spikes when mixing 250 short streams + 6 concurrent 512-token batched jobs. Additional clue: telemetry indicates a recent config change on 2026-03-08 that reduced burst capacity headroom in pool nid-dedicated-37.

SRE action so far: - Enabled temporary increased burst headroom for nid-dedicated-37 at 2026-03-10T03:05 UTC. - Adjusted allocator lock timeout from 250ms -> 100ms in a canary on staging. - Captured GPU kernel queue traces and memory defragmentation events and uploaded to artifact store (link in comment).
workaround: Short-term: (1) increase burst_headroom for the affected pool to allow immediate transient scale-outs; (2) schedule large batch jobs on isolated maintenance nodes or move them to off-peak windows; (3) for customers requiring low p99, recommend pinning small-stream routes to a dedicated subset of slots. Applied change: burst_headroom increased for nid-dedicated-37 at 2026-03-10T03:05 UTC — reduced p99 by ~60% in the first 10 minutes of observation.
resolution_notes: In-progress. Next steps: implement allocator improvement to prefer compacting small-stream slots proactively (design doc in PR), relax autoscaler admission rate-limits for short windows (feature flag), and add an automated policy that detects mixed-workload surges and forces temporary isolation of large-batch jobs. Planned deployment: autoscaler rate-limit change will be rolled out to canary on 2026-03-14 and to prod on 2026-03-17 pending validation.
